channel.title: Lockstep Arcade devlog
channel.description: News from the development of Lockstep Arcade

item.title: The satisfaction of people getting stuck into and completing hard levels
item.description:
So campaigns are a pretty new feature, it is difficult to make enough different levels to fill up a campaign properly, and I have included some levels at the end of the Spirits campaign that are really too difficult.

The levels in question are a couple of 'beam dance' levels, where crawlers move around an outer wall shooting deadly beams you need to avoid into the space you move through. The beams are obstructed by features inside the space and you need to take advantage of this, and the pattern that results as the crawlers move, to complete the level.

The challenge is then to activate a bunch of switches in sequence, each one opening up access to another switch, with the last switch eventually opening up access to the exit. (This is unashamedly derivative of an N++ level I enjoyed playing a lot with some friends!) Actually, these levels were originally designed to be played by multiple players working together, with the players coordinating to each activate different switches, but they could theoretically be completed by just one player, so I put them in as super challenging 'boss' levels to come up against at the end of the campaign.

I had tried the hardest level in 2 player co-op with my daughter. We found it challenging, had not yet managed to complete it, and were intending to come back to it.

I have had some people testing the Spirits campaign, then, through the Play2Review site, where they post gameplay recordings of their sessions. Actually, I hadn't looked at the review there yet, and had instead noticed a whole load of new games listed in the played games list, clicked through these and saw a player basically sieging these hard levels and eventually completing them. Another player also completed all the levels later on.

It is a really nice feeling, as a game designer, to see players succeed at a really hard level, I think. :)

Here is a video of a playthrough of the easier of the two levels:

And then here is a playthrough of the hardest level:

Other players obviously found the hardest level much too hard, and there is not enough of a gradual increase in difficulty through the Spirits campaign, so these two levels really represent a far from ideal difficulty cliff, but it is such a great feeling to see these levels completed that I am going to struggle not to include more hard levels like this in the future, I think. :)

I guess the solution will be 1) to add more levels that gradually ramp towards this difficulty (obviously), and 2) to communicate that these levels are really difficult so players are not surprised by this, and can choose whether or not to accept the challenge. (I am thinking for example, that there could be a difficulty rating as a number of stars, going from 1 to 5 stars, and then for really hard levels this could change from 5 stars to 5 skulls, or something like that.)

item.title: Placing stuff conditionally, campaign mode, fast retry
item.description:
Ok, so the main thrust of recent development has been a kind of 'campaign mode'.

Before this, after you completed the tutorial and went into the online part of the game, you would just choose from a big bag of playable levels. In testing videos, or when watching people playing, I would then see everyone just essentially start with the first in the list, or one they like the sound of, neither of which is likely to actually be the best map to start off with.

Apart from being difficult, most testers play single player, and the first level I saw people playing was actually not completable by a single player.

In this level, for Spirits, there is a mine blocking the narrow gap leading to the exit at the end of the level. This is a kind of cliché copied from N++. The point is that the level is actually designed for two players. The first player to reach the exit can then detonate this mine, dying in the process, but opening up the way for the second player to complete the level.

To make things worse, the config let me specify the different player counts the level was intended for, but the actual interface you would see would just tell you something about the level 'not being eligible for highscores'.

Of course, that interface could be improved, and a mechanism could be added to prevent you playing this level single player, but that's just more friction, and less possibilities for the player, and I was able to find a much better solution for this.

The solution, as shown in this screenshot of the level editor was to add the possibility to make things placed in the world conditional. So, in this case, that mine is only actually added if there is actually more than one player. (This way, the map actually becomes playable in this case.)

I also added the possibility to make placed items conditional on difficulty, since this also fits well with the idea of conditional placement. Taken together, these two conditional placement conditions then really help with generating a set of different maps to fill out a campaign, without having to do things like copying and modifying maps for these kinds of detail tweaks.

Campaign mode

The new campaign mode is very strongly inspired by the grid of levels in the N++ campaign, and I like the idea, in particular, that you get a kind of branching structure from this, and some choice about how exactly you prefer to proceed through the levels in the campaign.

So you start off with only the top left level in a grid being unlocked, and as you start to complete levels, the levels to the right and below the completed levels then also become available to play.

I recently added a thumbnail generation feature, which does a trick with creating a temporary game session, calling the normal render() method for the game, and capturing the resulting image in a texture for use as a thumbnail.

I modified this to add some caching and limit the number of new thumbnails that can be generated on any frame to 2, and then a thumbnail image can be rendered for each grid element in the campaign. (Locked elements get no thumbnail, and you just see a grey rectangle with a question mark, for these.)

The actual lobby mechanism didn't need any modifications to support this, initially. (I had previously added the possibility to change map selection in an active game room, which was actually the main prerequisite for this.)

I did add the possibility to create 'invite only' rooms, since there is a good chance you want to be able to choose who you want to play with, for an online co-op campaign. This was fairly complicated, but is also now available for 'normal' multiplayer rooms, and is a good thing to have, I think.

Fast retry loop after failed attempts

Apart from that, one thing I really wanted to improve was to make it much easier for players to retry a level after failure.

The point is that, as with N++, there is an intention that the levels can get pretty hard, but they don't take long to play, and then it really is supposed to be "if at first you don't succeed, try, try again".

In the previous release, after dying, you would get:

  1. The game end screen with the results, shown in game (click to move on)
  2. A post game results screen showing things like highscore updates (very nice to have if you actually got a highscore, but a pain when you just failed, click again to move on)
  3. Back in the game lobby, but you need to indicate you are ready, before the host can retry (if they actually agree)
  4. The host then needs to actually start the game

It took a lot of thinking to find some way to really cut back that sequence, without redesigning all the lobby server and client interactions, but now, on the client side you get the following shown after a game ending in failure:

And then, on the host side, after a short delay to give other players the chance to quit out if they want, you get:

Map 'nominations'

The one thing left for the campaign rooms, to make things work for co-op players not also on voice chat, was to give non-host players some way of indicating which map/level they would like to play next.

The design chosen for this was for non-host players to be able to 'nominate' which map they would like to play. This nomination is then purely informational, and the host can choose to take it into account or ignore it, but the non-host players nevertheless remain able to click ready or not click ready.

item.title: Improve your game
item.description:
(Changes for a submission to the 'Improve your game' jam.)

As it often works out, I started out with a number of improvements in mind very much targetting the gameplay side, and ended up spending a lot of time on in depth work on the underlying platform.

I wanted to make a number of improvements to the Serpents game with the theme of helping the game to play out more often in a way where players actually end up moving around the tails of other serpents.

(In play testing, instead, people would tend to collide a lot, not really build up a long tail, and then, when players did build up a long tail they would tend to just then be moving around the arena mostly by themselves.)

The basic ideas for these improvements are:

  1. Make it easier for players to control the Serpents (so that they collide less, and then tend to build up longer tails)
  2. 'Close' the player exits until players build up a tail of a given minimum length (so players can't just collect a couple of stars and cash this in directly)
  3. Take actions to encourage players to be in the same part of the arena more

For the first point, there turned out to be a very simple change that could help with this a bit, which is to reduce the maximum speed of serpents. Serpents that move slower are easier to control, and will collide less, and, while it was already possible to get your serpent to move more slowly, this takes a bit of finesse, and it is easy for the serpent speed to get out of control when you are trying to manoeuvre.

Because I kind of like the skill involved in moving the serpent around at higher speeds, I didn't then want to lose this completely, so I felt the need to add in a speedup pickup, which gradually enables you serpent to get back to the previous maximum speed (and then go a bit faster than this, even). There were some tricky technical details to work out for this, but more on this later..

Closing the player exits until a threshold minimum tail length is reached was also quite a trivial change (but is still a good change for the theme of the improvements).

For the last point, my daughter suggested the idea of having parts of the map coloured in grey or red, as kind of no-go or penalty areas, to encourage players to congregate more in the remaining non-penalised areas. I really like the idea of doing something like this, and I think this will add more things that are going on in the game, and general interest, as well as encouraging players to congregate more, but this can get quite involved, and needs a lot of thought, whereas I was able to come up with a much easier change which also achieves the same fundamental purpose.

The trick here was just to move the exits, which were previously next to the player start positions in each corner of the arena, all next to each other in the centre.

Coming back to the speedup pickups, there turned out to some tricky details in implementing even something simple like this, due to the lockstep architecture, with delay.

The pickups are collected by the front of the serpent tail which is synchronised network state. The tail cannot immediately speed up, however, because the local serpent head has already moved a number of frames in front of the tail, and if the movement characteristics of the tail change immediately, the tail will no longer follow directly along the path taken by the head.

(It's kind of a recurring theme of working on these games, with the lockstep architecture, that something that should be quite simple turns out to need a fair amount of thought, and some tricksy solution.)

The solution, in this case, is to queue up the speed change for application to the tail 'delay frames' later. The local head gets this speed change immediately, however. The tail will then catch up to the head delay frames later on, and get the same speed change applied at that point, keeping things in synch..

item.title: Starting a devlog
item.description:
Ok, so I've been meaning to start a devlog, and I got a bit of an extra push to do this since this is required for the Improve my Game jam.

I'll be writing about:

  1. game design issues that come up in the specific context of multiplayer gaming using a lockstep networking architecture with deterministic simulation
  2. other game design issues completely unrelated to that :)
  3. multiplayer lobby development
  4. technical issues that come up with a project that uses SDL3 on emscripten
  5. technical and design issues that come up when developing a phone game

Don't hesitate to let me know if there is some specific aspect of Lockstep Arcade you would be interested in reading about.

and,

Watch this space!
